The Apocrypha. A collection of religious texts written between the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament, primarily during the Hellenistic period from roughly 300 to 100 BCE. Considered deuterocanonical or second-canon by Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, they are excluded from Protestant Bibles.

The Apocrypha includes books like Maccabees, Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, and Ecclesiasticus, or Ben Sira. The term apocrypha derives from Greek apokryphos, meaning hidden or obscure, reflecting their disputed authority. Written primarily in Greek and Hebrew during a period when the Jewish canon was not yet fully fixed, many of these texts address themes of martyrdom, divine wisdom, and resistance to foreign rule, especially Seleucid oppression.

The Maccabees recounts the Jewish revolt against Seleucid rule and the rededication of the Jerusalem Temple, events forming the basis for Hanukkah. Despite their name, these texts were never actually lost or hidden in intent—early Christian writers knew and quoted them as sacred literature. Catholic and Orthodox churches include them in their biblical canon, while Jewish and Protestant traditions exclude them. The distinction reflects different canonical decisions made by various religious communities as texts were gathered.

They are crucial to understanding intertestamental Jewish thought and history. The Apocrypha connect to the Hebrew scriptures forming the foundation of Jewish tradition, and represent developments in Jewish theology and identity following the Second Temple period. For Catholic and Orthodox Christians, they remain central to biblical tradition.
